enforcement_mechanism: No enforcement or sanctions. Implementation is monitored through the Digital Policy Committee's reports to Council (Section VIII(d), p. 11), practical implementation guidance (VIII(b)) and an information-exchange forum (VIII(c)) (see OECD005).

Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). For SMEs, including start-ups, the lower of the two applies (Art. 99(6), OJ p. 116). The Act sets maxima; Member States lay down the penalty rules and enforce them (Art. 99(1), OJ p. 115). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53; OJ p. 78); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91; OJ p. 102) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104; OJ p. 106).

No new enforcement mechanism. The principles are applied by existing regulators 'using the powers and resources available to them' (para 55, PDF p. 41). Government anticipates, but has not committed to, a statutory duty on regulators to 'have due regard' to the principles (para 57, PDF p. 42), and may not introduce it (para 59). Regulators are encouraged to integrate the principles into existing monitoring, investigation and enforcement processes (para 68, PDF p. 46).

No specific mechanism identified in the examined provision. The Guidelines rely on soft accountability mechanisms (public and peer scrutiny of transparency reports, self-certifications, internal policies, committee hearings, §2.5, PDF p. 33; peer monitoring and third-party audits, §2.5 Recommendations, PDF p. 35). MeitY 'may publish a schedule' for compliance with these measures within 9-12 months (PDF p. 33). Voluntary measures may later become mandatory baseline requirements enforced by regulators (§2.4, PDF p. 29).

No specific mechanism identified in the examined provision; the obligations themselves do not yet exist. Enforcement of existing laws is to be 'timely and consistent' (§2.5 Recommendations, PDF p. 35). Part 3 Action Plan lists 'Develop clear liability regimes across the AI value chain' as a short-term action (PDF p. 40).

Not applicable: this is a framework-building task, not a compliance duty. The linked AI incidents database (recommendation 2, PDF p. 32) is designed to encourage reporting 'without the threat of penalties' (PDF p. 29) and would feed evidence into the framework.

No specific mechanism identified. AISI's role is research, testing and advice; the Guidelines give it no powers to compel testing or impose sanctions. It provides risk assessments and 'updates on industry compliance' to TPEC and AIGG (PDF p. 38).

Existing statutory powers of sectoral regulators under their own laws; no new AI-specific sanctions or enforcement powers are created. The institutional framework maps regulators to 'Enforcing applicable laws and regulations', 'Supervising compliance' and 'Handling grievances' (PDF pp. 42-43). AIGG is to 'issue guidelines to ensure that firms are held accountable for compliance with local laws' (PDF p. 36).

Due-diligence obligation under the IT Rules: under rule 7, if an intermediary fails to observe the Rules, 'the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 79 of the Act shall not be applicable to such intermediary' (loss of safe-harbour protection), exposing it to liability under the IT Act and other law. Takedown and blocking powers under the IT Act also apply.

Loss of safe-harbour protection under section 79(1) of the IT Act, 2000, so that liability under the IT Act and other laws (including the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023) can attach to the intermediary for the content concerned.

Not applicable: an internal government function. Its outputs feed the central monitoring and evaluation function and may lead to advice that further intervention is needed (Box 3.1, PDF p. 49). It includes sharing 'risk enforcement best practices' (PDF p. 51).

Existing regulators' statutory powers only. Central monitoring and evaluation of the framework (Box 3.1, PDF p. 49). A possible future statutory 'due regard' duty on regulators (para 57), which would bind regulators, not businesses. Regulators must monitor and evaluate their own implementation (para 64, PDF p. 44).
None in the provision itself: a request from government to regulators, with no statutory basis. Regulators' existing statutory powers remain the route to enforcement.
None identified: an anticipated future intervention, with no duty, power or sanction created.

Periodic reporting to Council and peer exchange only. No sanctions, compliance assessment or dispute mechanism. The 2024 Report to Council found the Recommendation was 'being implemented by its Adherents' (p. 5).
